\begin{bankq}[id=SI02-P1-PHY-S1-Q01, source={Score-I - Test 02 (31 Dec 2021)}, paper=1, qno=1, type=single, subtopic={Surface tension}, answer={A}, answer_src=key, difficulty=4, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: mercury level correction with capillary depression in barometer | steps: capillary depression 2 S cos theta/(r rho g); true pressure from observed height plus depression; evaluate}]

Considering that this region is occupied by ideal gasses, the number of moles of the ideal gas will be :

[Given : Density of mercury = 13.6 g/cc, surface tension of mercury = 0.5 N/m, temperature = $37^\circ$C, $g=10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, universal gas constant = $R$, angle of contact of mercury on tube = $135^\circ$]
\bfig{130.1}{SI02_p1_phy_s1_q01_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$0.55\dfrac{\pi}{R}\times10^{-6}$}
\opt{B}{$1.2\dfrac{\pi}{R}\times10^{-6}$}
\opt{C}{$0.88\dfrac{\pi}{R}\times10^{-6}$}
\opt{D}{$1.6\dfrac{\pi}{R}\times10^{-6}$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=SI08-P1-PHY-S1-Q02, source={Score-I - Test 08 (09 Feb 2022)}, paper=1, qno=2, type=single, subtopic={Surface tension}, answer={A}, answer_src=key, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K1 S2 I2 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: surface tension force on a wire ring held by a soap film | steps: film pulls the ring on two surfaces; equilibrium of ring weight, buoyancy and tension; find tension or force; evaluate | I: soap film has two surfaces}]
A Lightweight thin wire ring hanging on a soap film that is held in a circular frame. The mass of the ring is $m$, its radius $R$, the coefficient of surface tension of the film is $\sigma$, the diameter of the frame $D>2R$. The frame and ring are horizontal, their centres are on the same vertical line. What is the distance from the plane of the ring to the plane of the frame? Mass of the film can be neglected in comparison with the mass of the ring, Also $mg\ll\sigma R$.
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$h=\dfrac{mg}{4\pi\sigma}\ln\dfrac{D}{2R}$}
\opt{B}{$h=\dfrac{mg}{4\pi\sigma R}\left(\dfrac{D}{2}-R\right)$}
\opt{C}{$h=\dfrac{mg}{2\pi\sigma R}\left(\dfrac{D}{2}-R\right)$}
\opt{D}{$h=\dfrac{mg}{4\pi\sigma}\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{D}{2R}\right)$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

A horizontal plate is in equilibrium above a source of water jet at a height $h$ as shown in the figure. The water splashes parallel to the plate and does not rebound. The gravitational force on the plate is balanced by the force exerted by the jet of water. If the plate is displaced by a small distance in the vertically downward or upward direction, it is seen to execute SHM with a time period $T$. Find $T$ (in sec.). The speed of jet when it strikes the plate is $\dfrac{40}{\pi}$ m/s.
\bfig{184.6}{SI08_p1_phy_s4_q09_1.png}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=SI09-P1-PHY-S2-Q10, source={Score-I - Test 09 (16 Feb 2022)}, paper=1, qno=10, type=multi, subtopic={Pressure}, answer={A,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: water filled tube moving down, a constant acceleration | steps: effective gravity g - a; pressure at the base; hole efflux; check statements | I: acceleration changes effective gravity in the tube}]

Let $\beta=(P_1-P_2)/(\rho g d)$, where $\rho$ is density of water, $d$ is the inner diameter of the tube and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity. Which of the following statement(s) is(are) correct ?

\opt{B}{$\beta>0$ when $a=g/\sqrt2$}

\opt{D}{$\beta=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$ when $a=g/2$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

When water is filled carefully in a glass, one can fill it to a height $h$ above the rim of the glass due to the surface tension of water. To calculate $h$ just before water starts flowing, model the shape of the water above the rim as a disc of thickness $h$ having semicircular edges, as shown schematically in the figure. When the pressure of water at the bottom of this disc exceeds what can be withstood due to the surface tension, the water surface breaks near the rim and water starts flowing from there. If the density of water, its surface tension and the acceleration due to gravity are $10^3$ kg m$^{-3}$, 0.07 Nm$^{-1}$ and 10 ms$^{-2}$, respectively, the value of $h$ (in mm) is \underline{\hspace{1.5cm}}.-
\bfig{77.9}{SI11_p1_phy_s3_q02_1.png}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI11-P2-PHY-S3-Q02, source={Score-I - Test 11 (27 Feb 2022)}, paper=2, qno=2, type=numerical, subtopic={Bernoulli}, answer={9}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K2 S3 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: pressure drop around a train moving, a tunnel | steps: in train frame air flows past at speed relative; continuity S0 v = (S0 - St) v'; Bernoulli between front and sides; p0 - p = (1/2) rho (v'^2 - v^2); solve N}]

A bubble has surface tension $S$. The ideal gas inside the bubble has ratio of specific heats $\gamma=\dfrac53$. The bubble is exposed to the atmosphere and it always retains its spherical shape. When the atmospheric pressure is $P_{a1}$, the radius of the bubble is found to be $r_1$ and the temperature of the enclosed gas is $T_1$. When the atmospheric pressure is $P_{a2}$, the radius of the bubble and the temperature of the enclosed gas are $r_2$ and $T_2$, respectively. Which of the following statement(s) is(are) correct?
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{If the surface of the bubble is a perfect heat insulator, then $\left(\dfrac{r_1}{r_2}\right)^5 = \dfrac{P_{a2}+\dfrac{2S}{r_2}}{P_{a1}+\dfrac{2S}{r_1}}$}
\opt{B}{If the surface of the bubble is a perfect heat insulator, then the total internal energy of the bubble including its surface energy does not change with the external atmospheric pressure.}
\opt{C}{If the surface of the bubble is a perfect heat conductor and the change in atmospheric temperature is negligible, then $\left(\dfrac{r_1}{r_2}\right)^3 = \dfrac{P_{a2}+\dfrac{4S}{r_2}}{P_{a1}+\dfrac{4S}{r_1}}$.}
\opt{D}{If the surface of the bubble is a perfect heat insulator, then $\left(\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^{5/2} = \dfrac{P_{a2}+\dfrac{4S}{r_2}}{P_{a1}+\dfrac{4S}{r_1}}$.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

(II) & $h(r_0)$ & (Q) & $\dfrac{\left(1+\frac{\omega_0^4r_0^2}{4g^2}\right)^{3/2}}{\frac{\omega_0^2}g}$ \\
\hline
(III) & $\rho\left(\dfrac{r_0}2\right)$ & (R) & $\dfrac{\omega_0^2r_0^2}{2g}$ \\
\hline
(IV) & $\rho(0)$ & (S) & $\dfrac g{\omega_0^2}$ \\
\hline
 & & (T) & $\dfrac{2g}{\omega_0^2}$ \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\begin{qoptions}

\begin{bankpassage}[id=SRGBT07-P1-PHY-S1-G15-16, source={SRGBT - Test 07 (05 Sep 2021)}, questions={15-16}]
The fact that the density of ice is smaller than the density of water has an important consequence for homeowners, who have to contend with the possibility of bursting water pipes during severe winters. Water often freezes in a section of pipe exposed to unusually cold temperatures. The ice can form an immovable plug that prevents the subsequent flow of water, as Figure illustrates. When water (larger density) turns to ice (smaller density), its volume expands by 10\%. When ice forms on the right side of the plug, the expanding ice pushes liquid to the right. But it has nowhere to go if the faucet is closed. As ice continues to form and expand, the water pressure between the plug and faucet rises. The bulk modulus of ice is much more than that of the water. So water gets compressed. Even a small increase in the amount of ice produces a large increase in the pressure. Therefore, the pipe can burst at any point where it is structurally weak. There is a simple way to prevent pipes from bursting. Simply open the faucet, so it drips a little. The excessive pressure will be relieved.\par
\bfig{137.4}{SRGBT07_p1_phy_s0_q14_2.png}
\end{bankpassage}

Water can be considered to be electrically conducting; its surface tension is $\sigma$ and its density is $\rho$. A droplet of radius $r$ hangs below the nozzle. The radius grows slowly in time until the droplet separates from the nozzle due to the free fall acceleration $g$. Always assume that $d\ll r$.\par

\bfig{66.3}{TOAS12_p1_phy_s1_q05_1.png}

\opt{C}{Relative to the far-away surroundings, the pipe's electrostatic potential is $\phi$. the charge $Q$ of a drop when its radius is $r$, $Q=4\pi\varepsilon_0\phi r$}
\opt{D}{Consider the situation in which $r$ is kept constant and $\varphi$ is slowly increased. The droplet becomes unstable and breaks into pieces if the hydrostatic pressure inside the droplet becomes smaller than the atmospheric pressure, the critical potential $\varphi_{\max}$ at which this will happen $2\sqrt{\dfrac{\sigma r}{\epsilon_0}}$.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

One pan of balance holds a glass of water and stand from which a weight is suspended as in figure, what will not happen to balance's equilibrium if we lengthen the string so as to immerse the weight in the water?\par
\bfig{286.9}{NUR04_p1_phy_s2_q06_1.png}

\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{Equilibrium will be disrupted since buoyant force acting on weight decreases tension in the string so the pressure of the stand on balance decrease}

\opt{C}{The equilibrium of the balance will be preserved irrespective of position of weight}
\opt{D}{Instead of lengthening string If you put your finger in the glass of water without touching the walls and the bottom of the glass then also equilibrium will preserved}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
